open.speaker: harmon
lines: Harmon's. Anything you can't find I've got in the back, and if I haven't, Lonnie across the street has it used.
You're the Sutton folks. Marlene sends everybody over for film and I'm out of film. The suits took the last of it.
He's got a book on the counter. Look at the book.

passives.line: The ledger on the counter is open to November 1966. His father's hand, not his. He's been reading it, not writing in it.
Eleven in 1967. He was on this street when the bridge went. He talks fast so nobody asks.

options.text: Your dad kept this store before you.

fail.line: Dad kept it. Now I keep it. That's the family history; you want more, there's a plaque at the courthouse.

options.text: (Stand at the counter and say nothing.)

slow.speaker: harmon
lines: Slow since Tuesday. Suits came through and bought gloves, a map, chalk. Then Dwight Mason came in and bought nothing.
Stood by the batteries ten minutes. Then said 'Tell Harmon's boy I said goodbye.' I'm Harmon's boy. He was looking right at me.
He was saying goodbye to the store. Not to you.

father.speaker: harmon
lines: Dad. Forty-one years. He ran it through the '66 business and the bridge and the flood, and he kept the book the whole way.
Wrote down what everybody bought. Said in a town this size the book's the only honest newspaper.
A ledger is a primary source. I'll take a ledger over a headline.

counter_quiet.speaker: harmon
lines: Fine. Nobody does. Stand there, it's warm.
He's relieved. Look at his shoulders.

hub.speaker: harmon
lines: Well. Batteries are by the door and the book's on the counter, and only one of 'em's for sale.

static.line: He said forty-one years and his eyes went to December. There's a page he doesn't turn. Make him turn it.

options.text: That page is November 1966. Who bought reflectors that November?
You were eleven. Where were you when the bridge went?
This map came off your rack. Who marked the plant?
We'll let you get back to it.

science.speaker: harmon
lines: Bobby Kessler. Science. Kid couldn't spell it, so I spelled it for him and he copied it onto his hand.
Every red reflector on the shelf. I ordered more. They haven't sold. Nobody in this town wants a red light on their bike now.
That's a detail. That's a good detail.

ledger_1966.speaker: harmon
lines: ...Ray Kessler. Bobby's daddy. A dozen red reflectors and a sheet of plywood. Dad wrote 'a project'.
Look at the date. The 18th. The Register ran the two couples on the 16th. Ray bought his the week after.
He made a joke of it. He didn't start it. Dad underlined the date. I don't think he liked what it meant either.
Then the board explains the joke, and nothing before the 16th. Noted.

ledger_fail.speaker: harmon
lines: That's my dad's hand and my dad's business. The page was open because I was looking, not because you were.
Lonnie keeps books too. Go read his.

bridge_truth.speaker: harmon
lines: At the register. Dad went out the door at the sound and I stayed with the drawer because he told me to.
He came back at midnight with his hands wrong. Never said a word about it. The book's got nothing for December 15th.
Only blank page in forty-one years. I look at it sometimes. That's all. I look at it.
A blank page is a kind of marker, dear. Some people can't carve one.

bridge_fail.speaker: harmon
lines: You come in here for batteries, buy batteries. You come in for that, there's a memorial on the riverbank with forty-six names on it.

passives.line: That was the right question and the wrong day. You hear the bell on the door and it's you going out.

map.speaker: harmon
lines: That's my map. Dollar ninety-five, pencil mark's free. The suit bought it Tuesday with the gloves and the chalk.
Opened it on the counter and circled the plant before he'd paid. Didn't look for it. Knew where it was.
Asked did I remember him. I was eleven in 1967. I said no. He said 'That's all right, Mr Harmon. You did.'
He didn't blink when he said it, did he.
